'''Morris Kline''' (May 1, 1908 – June 10, 1992) was a professor of [[mathematics]] who wrote extensively on the [[history of mathematics|history]], [[philosophy of mathematics|philosophy]], and teaching of that subject. He was also a popularizer of mathematics.

== Early life and education ==
Kline was born to a Jewish family in [[Brooklyn]] on May 1, 1908,<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |date=August 4, 2025 |title=Kline, Morris, 1908-1992 |url=https://id.loc.gov/authorities/names/n80015674.html |access-date=June 1, 2026 |website=Library of Congress}}</ref> and resided in [[Jamaica, Queens]].  After graduating from [[Boys High School (Brooklyn)|Boys High School]] in Brooklyn, he studied mathematics at [[New York University]], earning a bachelor's degree in 1930, a master's degree in 1932, and a doctorate (Ph.D.) in 1936.<ref name=":3" /> He then spent two years, 1936 to 1938, at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in Princeton, New Jersey, where, he recalled, he learned considerable mathematics.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last=Alexanderson |first=G. L. |title=An Interview with Morris Kline: Part 2 |journal=[[The College Mathematics Journal|The Two-Year College Mathematics Journal]] |publisher=[[Mathematical Association of America]] |volume=10 |issue=4 |pages=259-64 |doi=10.2307/3026621}}</ref> 

== Career ==
After his time at the Institute for Advanced Study, Kline next worked at NYU as an instructor until 1942.<ref name=":3">{{cite book |title = Mathematical People: Profiles and Interviews |chapter = Morris Kline |year = 2008 |publisher = [[A K Peters]], Ltd. |isbn = 978-1-56881-340-0 |pages = 173–183 |first = G. L. |last = Alexanderson |author-link = Gerald L. Alexanderson |edition = 2nd |editor1 = Donald J. Albers |editor2 = Gerald L. Alexanderson }}</ref> Although he was originally trained in [[topology]] and worked as an assistant to [[James Waddell Alexander II|James Alexander]], Kline turned his attention to [[Differential equation|differential equations]] and [[applied mathematics]] after being convinced by [[Richard Courant]] that the greatest contribution a mathematician could make to society was to bring about the understanding of the world.<ref name=":4" /> He was influenced by the articles of [[Hermann Weyl]] for ''[[The American Mathematical Monthly]]'' and the works of [[Leonhard Euler]].<ref name=":4" />

During [[World War II]], Kline was posted to the [[United States Army Signal Corps|Signal Corps]] of the United States Army, and stationed at [[Belmar, New Jersey]]. Designated as a physicist, he worked in the engineering lab where [[radar]] was being developed. After the war, he continued investigating [[electromagnetism]], and from 1946 to 1966, he was director of the Division of Electromagnetic Research at the [[Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences]].<ref name=":4" />

After the war, Kline resumed his mathematical teaching at New York University, becoming a full [[professor]] in 1952. He taught at NYU until 1975. and wrote many papers and more than a dozen books on various aspects of mathematics and particularly the [[Mathematics education in the United States|teaching of mathematics]].<ref name=":1" /> He also published a textbook on calculus in 1967.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Satzer |first=William J. |date=November 21, 2015 |title=''Calculus: An Intuitive and Physical Approach'' |url=https://old.maa.org/press/maa-reviews/calculus-an-intuitive-and-physical-approach |access-date=March 20, 2026 |website=MAA Reviews |publisher=[[Mathematical Association of America]]}}</ref>

=== Writings on the teaching of mathematics ===
Kline repeatedly stressed the need to teach the applications and usefulness of mathematics rather than expecting students to enjoy it for its own sake.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Hechinger |first=Fred M. |date=April 15, 1986 |title=Danger of Mathematician Shortage |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1986/04/15/science/about-education-danger-of-mathematician-shortage.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150524191123/https://www.nytimes.com/1986/04/15/science/about-education-danger-of-mathematician-shortage.html |archive-date=May 24, 2015 |access-date=March 20, 2026 |work=The New York Times}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kline |first=Morris |date=February 1984 |title=''Curriculum Development in Mathematics'' by Geoffrey Howson, Christine Keitel, and Jeremy Kilpatrick |journal=[[The American Mathematical Monthly]] |volume=91 |issue=2 |pages=150-1 |doi=10.1080/00029890.1984.11971363}}</ref> He cautioned, however, that these applications must be carefully selected to suit the level of the course being taught and that at the introductory level, intuition, not [[Rigour#Mathematics|rigor]], should be the main focus.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Alexanderson |first=G. L. |date=June 1979 |title=An Interview with Morris Kline: Part 1 |journal=[[The College Mathematics Journal|The Two-Year College Mathematics Journal]] |publisher=Mathematical Association of America |volume=10 |issue=3 |pages=172-8 |doi=10.2307/3026737}}</ref> 

He issued multiple objections of how mathematics was taught in 1956,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kline |first=Morris |date=March 1956 |title=Mathematics texts and teachers: a tirade |journal=The Mathematics Teacher |publisher=[[National Council of Teachers of Mathematics]] |volume=49 |issue=3 |jstor=27955118}}</ref> 1966,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kline |first=Morris |date=December 1966 |title=Intellectuals and the Schools: A Case History |url=https://www.harvardeducationalreview.org/content/36/4/505 |journal=[[Harvard Educational Review]] |volume=36 |issue=4 |pages=505-511 |doi=10.17763/haer.36.4.w03116v23731080q|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and 1970,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kline |first=Morris |date=March 1970 |title=Logic versus Pedagogy |journal=[[The American Mathematical Monthly]] |volume=77 |issue=3 |pages=264-282 |doi=10.1080/00029890.1970.11992466}}</ref> as well as many of the textbooks written during this era.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last=Kline |first=Morris |date=October 1958 |title=The ancients versus the moderns, a new battle of the books |journal=The Mathematics Teacher |publisher=The National Council of Teachers of Mathematics |volume=51 |issue=6 |pages=418-27 |jstor=27955704}}</ref> For Kline, an appreciation for rigor took time to be developed and it was ill-advised to teach the abstract before the concrete.<ref name=":6" /> He was a vocal critic of the [[New Math]] movement to reform the teaching of mathematics.<ref name=":2" /> In 1973, he published the book ''[[Why Johnny Can't Add|Why Johnny Can't Add: the Failure of the New Math]]''. Its opening chapter is a [[parody]] of instruction as students' intuitions are challenged by the new [[jargon]] promoted by the New Math. He indicated that it was "practically impossible" to learn new mathematical creations without first understanding the old ones, and that "[[Abstraction (mathematics)|abstraction]] is not the first stage, but the last stage, in a mathematical development."<ref name="Kline">{{cite book |last=Kline |first=Morris |author-link=Morris Kline |title=Why Johnny Can't Add: The Failure of the New Math |title-link=Why Johnny Can't Add: The Failure of the New Math |publisher=[[St. Martin's Press]] |year=1973 |isbn=0-394-71981-6 |location=New York}}</ref>{{rp|17, 98}} Kline criticized the authors of the New Math textbooks, not for their mathematical faculty, but rather their narrow approach to mathematics, and their limited understanding of pedagogy and educational psychology.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gillman |first=Leonard |date=May 1974 |title=Review of ''Why Johnny Can't Add'' |journal=[[The American Mathematical Monthly]] |volume=81 |issue=5 |pages=531–2 |jstor=2318615}}</ref> Many other scholars were also critical of these reforms.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Mashaal |first=Maurice |title=Bourbaki: A Secret Society of Mathematicians |publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] |year=2006 |isbn=0-8218-3967-5 |language=French |translator-last=Pierrehumbert |translator-first=Anna |chapter=10: New Math in the Classroom}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Feynman |first=Richard P. |author-link=Richard Feynman |year=1965 |title=New Textbooks for the 'New' Mathematics |url=http://calteches.library.caltech.edu/2362/1/feynman.pdf |journal=Engineering and Science |volume=XXVIII |issue=6 |pages=9–15 |issn=0013-7812}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Simmons |first=George F. |author-link=George F. Simmons |title=Precalculus Mathematics in a Nutshell: Geometry, Algebra, Trigonometry |publisher=[[Wipf and Stock Publishers]] |year=2003 |isbn=978-1-59244-130-3 |page=}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=33}} [[Harry Schwartz (journalist)|Harry Schwartz]] wrote in his review of the book for ''[[The New York Times]]'': "Its significance goes far beyond its immediate topic. It raises the broader issue of how, in field after field in American life, there come to be sudden fixations on supposed [[wikt:panacea|panaceas]] for perceived problems. All too often, however, these panaceas turn out to have unforeseen consequences as bad as or worse than the original difficulties that triggered their adoption."<ref name=":1" />

In 1977, Kline turned to undergraduate university education with the title ''Why the Professor Can't Teach: The Dilemma of University Education''. Kline argues that the onus on professors in the United States to conduct research misdirects the [[scholarly method]] that characterizes good teaching. He lauded scholarship as expressed by expository writing or reviews of original work of others. For scholarship, he expects critical attitudes to topics, materials and methods. Kline reiterated [[E. H. Moore]]'s recommendation to combine science and mathematics at the high school level.<ref name="Kline" />{{Reference page|page=147}} This book was negatively received by D.T. Finkbeiner, [[Harry Pollard (mathematician)|Harry Pollard]], and [[Peter Hilton]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Finkbeiner |first=Daniel T. |last2=Pollard |first2=Harry |last3=Hilton |first3=Peter |date=May 1979 |title=Reviews |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00029890.1979.11994819 |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |volume=86 |issue=5 |pages=401-17 |doi=10.1080/00029890.1979.11994819|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Kline countered by complaining that many of these reviewers did not read the book but only a few excerpts from ''[[The Mathematical Intelligencer]]'' and noted that he had received many complimentary letters from instructors who shared his opinions and who resented the relentless pressure to undertake research, which came at the cost of good teaching.<ref name=":2" />

=== Writing on the history of mathematics ===
In 1972, Kline published his voluminous title ''Mathematical Thought from Ancient to Modern Times''. This book covers developments that have influenced mainstream mathematics from the times of [[ancient Babylon]], [[Ancient Egypt|Egypt]], and [[Ancient Greece|Greece]] up until the early twentieth century.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Schlapp |first=Robert |date=December 1973 |title=Morris Kline, ''Mathematical Thought from Ancient to Modern Times'' |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/proceedings-of-the-edinburgh-mathematical-society/article/morris-kline-mathematical-thought-from-ancient-to-modern-times-oxford-university-press-1973-xvii1238-pp-12/28EDC4A5790397C9853C49BC2B31627C |journal=Proceedings of the Edinburgh Mathematical Society |volume=18 |issue=4 |pages=340-1 |doi=10.1017/S0013091500010178}}</ref> Kline made frequent use of [[Primary source|primary sources]], especially in the later chapters.<ref name=":5" /> 

[[Gian-Carlo Rota]] praised Kline for reaching a compromise between depth and accessibility to the level of second-year undergraduate mathematics. Rota especially liked his treatment of classical topics such as [[Euclidean geometry]], but cautioned that his handling of more modern topics such as [[functional analysis]] was dated. Rota disagreed Kline's critical view of contemporary mathematical research, which, in Kline's opinion, overemphasized abstraction at the expense of utility.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rota |first=Gian-Carlo |date=September 1974 |title=Book Review: Morris Kline, ''Mathematical Thought from Ancient to Modern Times'' |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/bulletin-of-the-american-mathematical-society-new-series/volume-80/issue-5/Book-Review--Morris-Kline-Mathematical-thought-from-ancient-to/bams/1183535805.full |journal=[[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]] |volume=80 |issue=5 |pages=805-7}}</ref>

[[Ivor Grattan-Guinness]] indicated that while the book had a number of missed opportunities and technical errors or misinterpretations, this was nevertheless a strong presentation which dedicated much space—about half the book—to developments after 1800, which was unusual at the time of publication. He opined that Kline was at his best when discussing Euclidean geometry, [[calculus]], and the sociology of mathematics over the last three centuries, but faltered in [[Complex analysis|complex variables]], [[linear algebra]], and [[numerical analysis]]. He omitted [[probability theory]] and [[statistics]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Grattan-Guinness |first=Ivor |date=May 1973 |title=More Recent Mathematics: ''Mathematical Thought from Ancient to Modern Times'', Morris Kline |url=https://www.science.org/doi/full/10.1126/science.180.4086.627 |journal=Science |volume=180 |issue=4086 |pages=627-8 |doi=10.1126/science.180.4086.627|url-access=subscription }}</ref> 

[[Carl Benjamin Boyer]] also praised Kline for a detailed discussion of more recent developments in mathematics. Boyer especially praised Kline's handling of [[non-Euclidean geometry]] and his choice to cover topics not commonly found in other books on the history of mathematics, such as the [[Mathieu function|Mathieu functions]] and the [[Navier–Stokes equations]].<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last=Boyer |first=Carl B. |date=1974 |title=''Mathematical Thought from Ancient to Modern Times'', Morris Kline |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/351231 |journal=Isis |volume=65 |issue=1 |pages=104-6 |doi=10.1086/351231|url-access=subscription }}</ref> 

Lester Paldy deemed the book appropriate for teachers of physics as it contained a substantial amount of information on how mathematics had been applied to study physical phenomena.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Paldy |first=Lester G. |date=March 1974 |title=BOOK AND FILM REVIEWS: A Book for All Seasons: ''Mathematical Thought from Ancient to Modern Times'' |url=https://pubs.aip.org/aapt/pte/article-abstract/12/3/186/266297/BOOK-AND-FILM-REVIEWS-A-Book-for-All-Seasons |journal=The Physics Teacher |volume=12 |pages=186 |doi=10.1119/1.2350323|issue=3|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Writings on mathematical research ===
Kline urged that mathematical research concentrate on solving problems posed in other fields, such as physics and computer science. In his own words, "the greatest contribution mathematicians had made and should continue to make was to help man understand the world about him."<ref name=":1" /> In Chapter XIII of ''[[Mathematics: The Loss of Certainty]]'' ("The Isolation of Mathematics"), he deplored the way mathematical research was being conducted, complaining that often mathematicians were not willing to become acquainted with the (sometimes deep) context needed to solve applied problems in sciences, and instead prefer to invent [[pure mathematics]] that were not necessarily of any consequence. He also blamed the [[publish or perish]] academic culture for this state of affairs.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news |last=Pace |first=Eric |date=June 11, 1992 |title=Morris Kline, 84, Math Professor And Critic of Math Teaching, Dies |url=http://www.nytimes.com/1992/06/11/nyregion/morris-kline-84-math-professor-and-critic-of-math-teaching-dies.html |access-date=March 18, 2026 |work=The New York Times|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110617023122/http://www.nytimes.com/1992/06/11/nyregion/morris-kline-84-math-professor-and-critic-of-math-teaching-dies.html|archive-date=June 17, 2011}}</ref> William Barrett of ''The New York Times'' praised it as an "immensely readable" account of the decline of mathematics due to conflicting schools of thought.<ref name=":1" />

== Death ==
Kline died of [[heart failure]] at the [[Maimonides Hospital]] in Brooklyn, New York on June 10, 1992. He was 84 years old.<ref name=":7" /><ref name=":1" />
